prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

They flee from me that sometime did me seek With naked foot, stalking in my chamber. I have seen them gentle, tame, and meek, That now are wild and do not remember That sometime they put themself in danger To take bread at my hand; and now they range, Busily seeking with a continual change. Thanked be fortune it hath been otherwise Twenty times better; but once in special, In thin array after a pleasant guise, When her loose gown from her shoulders did fall, And she me caught in her arms long and small; Therewithall sweetly did me kiss And softly said, “Dear heart, how like you this?” It was no dream: I lay broad waking. But all is turned thorough my gentleness Into a strange fashion of forsaking; And I have leave to go of her goodness, And she also, to use newfangleness. But since that I so kindly am served I would fain know what she hath deserved.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker laments that those who once sought him out affectionately now avoid him and behave as strangers.
- He remembers a time when his lovers were gentle and trusting, willingly coming close to him.
- He recalls one especially intimate encounter in which a woman embraced and kissed him tenderly.
- The speaker insists that this experience was real, not a dream, but says it has now changed into abandonment.
- He reflects bitterly on being forsaken and wonders what his former lover deserves for her changeable behavior.
prompts.L4:

The poem explores the speaker’s abandonment by former lovers through a reflective contrast between past intimacy and present rejection. It finds that affection has turned into fickleness and betrayal, highlighting the instability of desire and the speaker’s bitter sense of injustice.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: They, With, That

outputs.L1:
Those who once sought me now flee from me, barefoot and stealthy in my chamber. I have seen them gentle, tame, and meek; now they are wild and no longer remember that they once placed themselves in danger to take bread from my hand. Now they wander restlessly, busily seeking continual change.

Thanks be to Fortune, it has been otherwise—twenty times better—but once especially: lightly dressed in a pleasing manner, when her loose gown fell from her shoulders, and she caught me in her long, slender arms. With that, she kissed me sweetly and softly said, “Dear heart, how do you like this?”

It was no dream; I lay fully awake. Yet all has been transformed, through my gentleness, into a strange manner of abandonment. By her kindness, I am permitted to go; and she, likewise, is free to pursue novelty. But since I have been served so graciously, I would gladly know what she has deserved.
outputs.L2:
Those who once came looking for me now run away.  
Barefoot, they used to move quietly through my room.  
I remember them as soft, obedient, and mild,  
but now they are untamed and seem to have forgotten  
that they once risked themselves  
to accept food from my hand. Now they wander elsewhere,  
restlessly searching, always wanting something new.

Still, I thank fortune, because things were once  
twenty times better than they are now—especially on one occasion.  
She was lightly dressed in a pleasing way,  
and as her loose gown slipped down from her shoulders,  
she caught me in her long, slender arms.  
Then she kissed me sweetly  
and gently asked, “Dear heart, how do you like this?”

It was not a dream; I was fully awake.  
But because of my kindness, everything has changed  
into a strange kind of abandonment.  
By her generosity, I am now allowed to leave,  
and she is free as well to chase novelty.  
Yet since I have been treated so graciously,  
I would very much like to know what reward she deserves.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back with sorrow on how dramatically his situation has changed. There was a time, he says, when the people who loved him sought him out with warmth and affection. They came to him willingly, treated him with tenderness, and seemed to trust him completely. Now, however, those same people avoid him. They pass him by as though they do not know him, behaving like strangers rather than former companions.

He remembers the past with particular vividness. In those earlier days, his lovers were gentle and open-hearted. They were not distant or suspicious, but drew near to him freely. Their affection seemed sincere, and their closeness gave him confidence that he was truly loved.

Among these memories, one intimate encounter stands out most clearly. He recalls a woman who once came to him with tenderness, embracing him and kissing him lovingly. The moment was filled with warmth and closeness, and it seemed to confirm the affection between them. For the speaker, this memory is not vague or uncertain; it remains powerful and emotionally real.

He insists that what he experienced was not a dream or an illusion. It truly happened, and he remembers it as something genuine. Yet that former intimacy has now been replaced by rejection. What once felt like love has turned into distance, silence, and abandonment.

Because of this change, the speaker feels deeply wounded. He reflects bitterly on the pain of being forsaken by someone who once showed him such affection. Her behavior seems unreliable and changeable, and he wonders what she deserves for treating him this way. His grief is mixed with anger, as he struggles to understand how tenderness could so completely turn into neglect.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker looking back on relationships that once seemed intimate, loyal, and emotionally secure, but which have now ended in abandonment. Its central movement is one of contrast: the speaker remembers a time when former lovers offered affection, tenderness, and devotion, yet now those same figures have withdrawn their love and turned away. This shift from closeness to rejection gives the poem much of its emotional force, as the speaker measures the warmth of the past against the coldness of the present.

As the poem develops, love is shown not as constant or dependable, but as unstable and changeable. The speaker’s former lovers appear fickle, capable of changing their feelings without warning and leaving behind the person they once cherished. What had seemed like sincere affection is now understood as unreliable, perhaps even deceptive. This creates a sense of betrayal: the speaker feels not only deserted, but wronged, as if promises or emotional bonds have been broken unfairly.

The tone of the poem is therefore reflective but also bitter. The speaker does not simply mourn lost love; they question the justice of being cast aside after having once been valued. Their pain comes from the contrast between what love appeared to be and what it has become. By emphasizing this change, the poem explores the insecurity of desire and the emotional damage caused when affection proves temporary. Ultimately, it portrays love as a force that can quickly turn from intimacy into rejection, leaving the abandoned speaker with resentment, disappointment, and a sharp sense of injustice.

They walked forward with a quiet confidence that made the whole room pause. They did not need to explain every step, because their actions spoke with a clarity that words often lacked. With patience, they listened; with courage, they acted; and with hope, they continued even when the path became difficult.

That was what made their journey meaningful. Not perfection, not speed, but the belief that every small effort mattered. They knew that challenges would come, but they also knew that together, with trust and determination, they could face whatever waited ahead.
